title: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club
summary: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club sits within the broader Shinnecock Hills landscape, part of Shinnecock ancestral territory and the land at the center of the 1703 lease and 1859 land-loss history. The course is also a place where Shinnecock labor, caddying, greenskeeping, and golf history are visible, including Oscar Bunn and generations of Shinnecock workers. The 2026 U.S. Open brings global attention back to this landscape, making source-grounded land acknowledgment especially important.
address_label: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club, Southampton, NY (general public course area)
ancestral_territory_note: Shinnecock Hills is documented in Shinnecock land-history sources as part of the lands covered by the 1703 lease and later 1859 land-loss dispute. The marker gives broad course-area context rather than a burial or other sensitive-site coordinate.
why_this_matters: The 2026 U.S. Open landscape is Shinnecock homeland, not only a famous golf course. It connects championship history to land loss, burial-ground disruption, and Shinnecock labor and skill: tribal members helped build and maintain the course, Oscar Bunn played in the 1896 U.S. Open, and later Shinnecock workers shaped the grounds across generations.
introduction_title: A Championship Course on Shinnecock Land
introduction_content:
Shinnecock Hills Golf Club is known internationally as one of golf's historic championship venues, but it also stands within the broader Shinnecock Hills landscape, part of Shinnecock ancestral territory. Shinnecock land-history sources connect this area to the 1703 lease and the 1859 loss of Shinnecock Hills lands. The course story therefore belongs with histories of land, labor, burial-ground disruption, and continuing Shinnecock presence.

The 2026 U.S. Open returns global attention to Shinnecock Hills from June 18-21, 2026. That attention should also hold the deeper history of the place, including Shinnecock workers, caddies, golfers, preservation advocates, and the continuing memory of Shinnecock land.
history_content:
In 1891, Shinnecock tribal members helped lay out the first course at Shinnecock Hills. Project sources describe 150 Shinnecock people assisting Willie Dunn with the first 12 holes. Those same sources record Dunn's own description that burial mounds were treated as golf features: some were left as bunkers and others were scraped out for sand traps. Materials from Sebonac and Woodland-period village contexts, including pottery and human remains, were removed to museums.

Shinnecock people were not only laborers in the course's construction. The cultural-history record describes Shinnecock men as greenskeepers, workers, and caddies from the beginning. Joshua Kellis is identified as a caddymaster, James Phillips appears in course-maintenance history, and Oscar Bunn is remembered as an early Shinnecock golf professional and craftsperson connected to the club.

In 1896, Oscar Bunn, a Shinnecock-Montaukett player, and John Shippen competed in the U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills after other players objected to their participation. Their presence belongs to both golf history and the longer story of race, Native presence, and labor around the course.
preservation_content: Shinnecock community members and allies have continued to call attention to Shinnecock Hills as ancestral land and to protect burial and sacred places across the region. In 2018, Shinnecock people protested during the U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills. In 2024, the Shinnecock Nation hosted Muwekma Ohlone Trail of Truth riders as part of a broader public statement about land, sovereignty, and dispossession.
land_loss_content:
Shinnecock land-history sources identify Shinnecock Hills as part of lands covered by the 1703 lease between Southampton trustees and the Shinnecock Nation. In 1859, approximately 4,422 acres were transferred out of Shinnecock control. A Shinnecock legal complaint alleged fraud, undue influence, and misrepresentation, but the case did not come to trial.

The present course area provides broad context for this history of land loss and continuing cultural concern. Burial and other sensitive locations are not identified.
vandalism_content: Project sources describe the golf course's early construction as a desecration of Shinnecock burial and village places in the Shinnecock Hills landscape. The public record should name that harm without exposing exact sensitive locations. The history therefore keeps the location broad and points readers to the source-cited historic moments for the dated record.
whereintheworld_content: The USGA identifies Shinnecock Hills Golf Club as the venue for the 126th U.S. Open, June 18-21, 2026, with a 156-player field on a 7,440-yard, par-70 course. The official fan guide also names Shinnecock Nation Reservation parking and the Shinnecock Nation Powwow Grounds as part of event logistics. Land acknowledgment around the 2026 championship belongs alongside Shinnecock land-loss history, including the 1703 lease and later 1859 dispute over Shinnecock Hills.
